children.text:
Driving a lean proof manually is a lot of effort. It's often 50x or 100x the effort of writing the initial program in the first place. The grand idea here is that if you can get a system to have a good heuristic/intuition for figuring out those proofs, you can lower this effort amplification by a lot. This makes formal verification at this level feasible for mission critical software, and also a larger slew of software we rely on.

The difficulty lies in coming up with the right formulations, and also some times altering the program to make it amenable to proof. It's quite often the case that a proof won't go through unless the program itself has the right idea.

As for the halting problem: it is highly theoretical. Lots of programs which are useful can be proven to halt for instance. Or you can just prove that the program is correct up to the point in time where the sun expansion covers the earth. There are often practical ways around such limitations, including the alteration or reformulation of the program.

children.author: gf000
children.text:
Formal verification is actually a very interesting concept and topic. There is a famous statement called the Curry–Howard correspondence: every type signature is a theorem, and the implementation is its proof.

So if I have a language where I can encode in the type system that a number is a prime and is even, then for example the following would be a theorem with a proof:

  Lemma even-prime: a -> Prime(a) ∧ Even(a) { // read as 'it returns a number `a` that is both prime and even 
    return 2
  }
If we restrict the language enough, we can both encode very complex statements and can make sure that one can only ever write an implementation that compiles if it's actually true. E.g. an ordinary language like python where you could return None instead of 2 would fail these requirements.

So they often have dependent type systems -- in these you can freely mix functions and values in your type signatures, not just types. E.g. you could have a Matrix type with two parameters, and then you can have functions like `transpose: Matrix a b -> Matrix b a`.

---

But this is just one side of the whole thing, the other is how to actually prove anything, like what even is `Even` in the above? A type like `someNum: Int` is also a theorem, but it only translates to "there exists an integer" - hardly interesting.

The real "mind blow" (at least to me) was that we just simply create a type for Equality. It takes the same parameter twice [1] (like in the Matrix example it would be Matrix a a) -- and thus we get a construct that can only be instantiated if the two sides are equal as per the language's compilers rules, that is automatically enforced by the compiler itself!

So now you can have `Eq 2 (1+1)`, but not `Eq 2 (1+3)`. And one last step that makes it general enough for all kinds of proofs, the compiler of these languages are not Turing complete. You can write many things, but for reasoning about loops you usually introduce a fuel that is always decreasing (and thus the compiler will accept it, as it knows it will run out once and that's enough for it). So it can evaluate everything, even in types and creating a normalized expression -- and then accepts everything as equal that normalizes to the same thing.

So for a more complex proof, you can just break down the problem to small steps that are by themselves understandably equal by the compiler.

[1] It's not quite true in this form

children.author: contravariant
children.text:
Dijkstra's approach would be to prove there is a strictly decreasing natural number associated to the loop.

This limits programs to the ones that can be formally shown to terminate. Which is good enough for most purposes.

My approach is to accept programs that run forever as long as I'm fairly sure each loop makes progress of some sort (instead of simply doing "while not solved: continue").

Edit: There's also a fun algorithm that, as far as I know, only provably terminates by being bounded by a sequence of strictly decreasing ordinals. Which breaks all kinds of models for proving it terminates.

children.text: You can model physical devices to arbitrary degrees of precision. Lanyon is doing it. These are not limitations of verification. Metrological models of semiconductor fabrication can even do verification over the distribution of faulty circuit outcomes.

You cannot formally verify heat-induced transistor stability issues, solar radiation, next-cell state change caused by EMF from adjacent cells (rowhammer)....

And while possible, good luck validating systems against intentional attacks-- fault injection, power tampering, bus attacks....

It is vital that "formally verified within X scope" does not turn into the leaky abstraction "is secure". Go watch Microsoft's talk on XBox security, and what they had to do to make it as secure as it is (primarily: tightly control hardware, code, and platform). It is not something you throw AI at, and it's not something that you can generalize to the entire computing world.
We can formally verify the Verilog or equivalent too.

> Most software verification is proved "for all possible inputs", e.g. the system maintains some invariant regardless of which sequence of actions is taken.

Without suggesting that this has no value-- it must be noted that such verification only applies on theoretical hardware and to the specific behavior in scope of the verification. Actual hardware is nondeterministic, and an algorithm can be correct while suffering from a side-channel.

> an AI agent is in the critical path in production i.e. non-deterministic action may occur(albeit with recovery)

Most software verification is proved "for all possible inputs", e.g. the system maintains some invariant regardless of which sequence of actions is taken. Those inputs could be from a user interacting with the software, or they could be API calls made to our library, etc. There's no reason you couldn't model an AI agent's choices in a similar way: i.e. prove that the desired invariants hold, for all possible sequences of actions the AI component might choose.

That might be straightforward, if the AI agent is constrained to pick from a simple set of domain-specific actions. In contrast, we can't say much about a system involving an AI agent with a full Bash shell.

> What scenarios does it make sense to have a lean proof from the start?

It's usually much easier to verify software that was written and structured with that in mind; rather than trying to reason about some arbitrary blob of code after-the-fact. So, if you do want to prove stuff, it should very much be in there from the start.

children.author: mobilejdral
children.text: Got a link?

I have been writing my own programming language _completely in lean_, from the parser down to the compiler.

My current workflow is i have a coordinating agent, and then a bunch of long running sessions that are specialized (CS theory, Kernel, Surface, Lowering/Backend, Corpus, Docs, etc). I only talk to the coordinator, they only accept tasks from the coordinator, but they can ask each other questions. None of them do their own coding, they assign coding tasks to agents/workflows. The main purpose of that is to stop it from blowing out context windows. Each has a million tokens of long term context and their own memory/claude.md etc, and they don't waste it by writing code directly. All work is assigned via github issues and answered with PRs. The coordinator mostly just keeps big picture goals in mind and manages PRs, etc..

I've currently got a fully formally verified borrow calculus and effect algebra, with a formally verified guarantee of memory safety and that all programs either continue (don't get wedged, no deadlocks), or they terminate with the heap empty. The only thing _not_ formally verified is the lowering to LLVM.

The language is mature to the point that I have real programs in it...

I have been experimenting with utilizing how easy it is for AI to code lean ( https://metamagic.substack.com/p/beyond-the-proof-dump-lean-...) and a few lessons

1. AI Lean is not perfect and AI can easily cheat given it is writing the lean. For anyone playing around with AI Lean code at minimum you need another adversarial prompt to review the ai generated lean.

2. In the paper poking around I see they did re-introduce some bugs to verify it would catch them, but they didn't find any bugs it looks like. Maybe signal is just amazing with many eyes reviewing it, but the real story for the rest of us is that if you start AI converting to Lean the value will be in what assumptions it finds. Even for stuff I thought was really logically tight, Lean found a few minor things I had to fix. Similar to fuzzing where I have never not found bugs when I introduced fuzzing into a codebase I expect the same for converting specs to lean.

3. Having the ability to generate Lean (cheaply) via AI is a very interesting unlock for coding. Potentially being able to go from spec to lean to code, using the lean as a logic gatekeeper has the potential to be a real capability that is used more everyday and not just in research.

From this I think it's a given that they were talking about the implementation, not the specification

> To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.

Of course, there are several official pieces of software which implement the specified Signal protocol, so it's not guaranteed they verified all of Signal's software which implements it https://github.com/signalapp/libsignal

I'd be surprised if there were no security bugs in any of the code here. It's more likely that they tested the implemented logic for creating/using the cryptographic primitives, than that they actually verified there were no bugs at all in the code

I'm actually unclear on whether they just translated some unmentioned design specification (whitepaper, maybe?) of the Signal protocol to Lean; or whether they actually translated the official app's implementation of the protocol to Lean.

I had assumed them to mean the latter, since I don't think the protocol design specification on its own would shake out into "over six million lines of Lean code." (Though if someone who knows Lean well thinks that's actually a reasonable number, please do correct me.) 6MM lines of proof code sounds more like something you get by "translating" an average-sized self-contained imperative-language library (like the protocol impl library) into a highly-rigorous prover language line-by-line, with a lot of the overhead coming from having to model imperative-language / imperative-CPU-target-abstract-machine semantics in rigorous mathematical form.

Annoyingly, the wording of the article is a bit too ambiguous to say for sure either way. They just say they "generated" the Lean code; they didn't say what it was being generated from.

I applaud them for starting with the protocol, because that can be generalized beyond any one specific implementation in principle, even if, in practice, we're somewhat limited to the official Signal apps given their centralized nature. Securing the applications themselves (perhaps starting with their implementations of the protocol, but the rest is also fair game) will inevitably be a bigger task.

children.author: dnautics
children.text:
is it just the protocol? Or is it also "the part of signal that implements the protocol", at least, yes it does what it's supposed to, with no weird timing collisions when multithreaded?

Also, I presume there are some unproved baked in assumptions about cryptographic primitives (e.g, but not necessarily, "sha512 has a uniform distribution")

Note that this is about Signal’s cryptographic protocol, not the Signal App or the surrounding platform OS.

Proofing and securing those is the way larger attack vector and work to come.

> they only proved narrow properties of the system.

It's that, yes.

They didn't prove that the code has no bugs; they proved that none of the current bugs (known or unknown) are security-breaking bugs, per their formalized security model.

> First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.

The generated Lean code here is just being checked against the "formal mathematical specifications of Signal's security goals", not checked for the low-level properties you might care about as a programmer, e.g. "will it ever leak memory" or "will it ever crash", etc. And in fact, the code is not even being checked for the reachability of non-security-violating protocol failure states, e.g. "could the protocol ever deadlock such that neither side can send messages any more".

It's still perfectly possible for the code to have all of these problems. It's now just known that, as of the commit they did this analysis against, none of those low-level problems, as far as they exist in the codebase, can cause a security-model violation.

Or, to put that another way: the system has been proven to "fail safe" in all its current failure modes, per their specific definition of safety (which is basically "keeping to the security guarantees Signal markets itself to users as having".)

Very cool. A couple of years back I was toying with the thought of developing a specialized model for formal verification using something like the AlphaZero approach. Given the news from the past few months now I'm glad that I didn't, it really seems that general purpose LLMs are eating everything.

Interesting that they end up with 26k lines of specifications (including Arm semantics). That's quite a large trusted computing base. I guess they need to develop the symbolic/computational models from the ground up. It'll be interesting to see if we can develop reusable libraries of these, a la mathlib, and how the incentives work out there. The AI labs are probably not particularly interested in this, and it's also likely to be thankless work for the researchers. But perhaps if companies doing verification or selling verified products do sprout out, maybe there will have an incentive to share the work and have a standardized TCB. That might, for better or worse, also put a practical end to the "interactive theorem prover wars".

It's also interesting how this will play work for code under development. ChatGPT claims that the day after this was released, libsibnal changed substantially :D Perhaps an intermediate-level, untrusted model in Rust could help (where most of the proof relates the Rust model to the spec, and then a more mechanical proof relates the Rust model to the binary); seL4 did this a long time ago. But I've no idea if this is practical, I haven't heard of anything encoding (full) Rust semantics into an interactive theorem prover... not that it's possible to keep up with the news these days anyway, especially if it's not your full time job. Another question that I don't know the answer to is how full-program optimization changes the picture with that, wonder if someone has any insights there.
